prompt.context: Your client produces strawberry jam for the US market. It experienced declining profits last year. Roland Berger has been hired to investigate what causes the decline in profitability and what to do about it. Industry profitability has been stable. The client is the market leader and has the strongest brand. Competition is unchanged from previous years. The client has been profitable in 2008 and before; only in 2009 has profitability been disappointing. Consumers are price sensitive but brand loyal.
prompt.question: What causes the decline in profitability and what should the client do about it?

clarifying_info.q: What does the client's product mix look like?
clarifying_info.a: Before 2009 the client only produced standard-shaped jars (small, medium, large). In 2009 the client introduced a belly-shaped jar. The belly-shaped jar has the same size as the medium standard jar and sells at the same price as the medium standard jar.

clarifying_info.q: Has anything changed in production or distribution?
clarifying_info.a: When introducing the belly-shaped jar, the speed of the filling line had to be reduced to prevent jars from breaking. This led to the necessity of overtime for line operators. Additionally, belly-shaped jars take more room per jar on trucks and are more likely to break during shipping than medium standard jars.

clarifying_info.q: What is the profitability of the belly-shaped jar vs. the standard medium jar?
clarifying_info.a: Profit on the belly-shaped jar and the medium standard jar is identical (same price, but higher costs for the belly-shaped jar imply lower margin).

exhibits.title: Reasons for Declining Profitability — Value Chain
exhibits.shows: A value chain framework prompting the candidate to identify where the change in product mix negatively affects profitability, covering production and distribution stages
exhibits.data: Production: filling line speed reduction, overtime costs. Distribution: higher truck space per jar, higher breakage rate during shipping.

framework: Diagnose the profit decline: revenue side (price, volume, mix) vs. cost side (COGS, SGA, distribution)
Isolate the timing: profitability was fine through 2008; declined only in 2009 — align with the belly-jar launch
Map the value chain of the jam manufacturer to pinpoint where the new product mix hurts economics
Quantify the impact: production cost increase (overtime) and distribution cost increase (space + breakage)
Formulate a recommendation: eliminate the belly-shaped jar, reprice it, or redesign production/distribution to restore margins

questions.prompt: Why did profitability decline? Walk through the value chain since the belly-shaped jar was introduced.
questions.guidance: A strong answer traces the problem through production (slower fill speed → overtime labor cost) and distribution (more truck space per unit → higher logistics cost per jar; higher breakage → waste and spoilage cost). The candidate should note that revenue per jar is unchanged (same price as medium standard) while costs rose, compressing margin.

questions.prompt: Given that the belly-shaped jar sells at the same price as the medium standard jar but carries higher costs, what is the implication for profitability?
questions.guidance: Even though stated profit is 'identical' at face value, the hidden costs (overtime, excess truck space, breakage) make the true economic profit of the belly jar lower than the standard medium jar. The candidate should articulate that the product mix shift toward belly jars diluted overall company margin.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the reasons the belly-shaped jar caused a decline in profitability? Run through the value chain of the jam manufacturer.

categories.name: Production
ideas: Filling line must run slower to prevent jar breakage — reduces throughput
Reduced throughput requires overtime for line operators — raises labor cost per unit
Potential re-tooling or changeover costs for the new jar shape

categories.name: Distribution
ideas: Belly-shaped jars have a larger footprint per jar on trucks — fewer jars per truckload, higher cost per jar shipped
Higher breakage rate during shipping — increases spoilage/waste cost and may trigger customer service issues
Potentially higher packaging cost to protect the fragile belly shape

categories.name: Procurement / Input Costs
ideas: Belly-shaped jars may cost more to source than standard jars
Specialized jar procurement could reduce economies of scale on standard jars

categories.name: Revenue / Pricing
ideas: Belly-shaped jar priced the same as medium standard — no price premium to offset higher costs
Consumers are price-sensitive, limiting ability to raise price retroactively

recommendation: Eliminate the belly-shaped jar: it generates the same revenue as the medium standard jar but carries higher production and distribution costs, making it margin-dilutive; since consumers are brand loyal, they are likely to switch back to standard jars without significant volume loss

If elimination is not preferred, restructure production (invest in a filling line capable of handling belly jars at full speed) and distribution (optimize packing configuration or switch to sturdier packaging) to close the cost gap

If structural cost fixes are feasible, a modest price premium on the belly-shaped jar (positioning it as a premium/gifting SKU) could restore margins, but price sensitivity of consumers limits this lever
risks: Eliminating the belly jar cedes differentiation ground; competitors could introduce a similar jar and capture brand-loyal consumers who prefer it
A price increase on the belly jar may accelerate volume decline given consumer price sensitivity
Production investments to fix the filling line require upfront capital with uncertain payback timeline
next_steps: Conduct a detailed cost-per-unit analysis for belly jar vs. standard medium jar to quantify the margin gap precisely
Survey or test consumer reaction to discontinuation of the belly jar vs. a price increase
Evaluate capital cost of upgrading the filling line against the NPV of retaining the belly jar SKU
